syllabus_version.title: CBSE Curriculum for the Academic Year 2026-27

topics.title: A Lakh Varieties and Getting a Feel of Large Numbers

concepts.learning_objective: Recognise one lakh as 1,00,000, the smallest 6-digit number, and compare quantities with it.
Get a sense of large measurements by comparing them with familiar quantities.

topics.title: Reading and Writing Numbers in the Indian System

concepts.learning_objective: Place commas in the Indian place value system and identify the place of each digit.
Convert between numerals and number names using lakhs and thousands.

topics.title: Land of Tens: Place Value through Button Clicks

concepts.learning_objective: Find how many presses of +10, +100 or +1000 buttons make a given number.
Explain why the fewest button clicks for a number equals the sum of its digits.

topics.title: Of Crores and Crores: Indian and American Systems

concepts.learning_objective: Relate thousand, lakh, crore and arab and count the zeroes in each.
Read, write and compare numbers in the Indian and American (International) systems.
Decide when rounding up or rounding down is appropriate in a real situation.
Find the nearest thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh and crore of a number.
Estimate sums and differences of large numbers and judge which estimate is closer.
Regroup factors such as 5 = 10/2 and 125 = 1000/8 to multiply quickly.
Predict the possible number of digits in a product from the digits of its factors.

topics.title: Did You Ever Wonder...? Thought Experiments

concepts.learning_objective: Make reasonable assumptions to test whether a large-number claim is possible.
Carry out large calculations in stages to answer distance and time questions.
Find the value of a simple arithmetic expression and recognise that different expressions can have the same value.
Write an arithmetic expression that describes an everyday situation.
Compare two expressions using =, < or > according to their values.
Compare sums and differences by reasoning about how the numbers differ, without full calculation.
Use brackets to show which operation in an expression is done first.
Identify the terms of an expression by writing subtractions as additions of inverses.

topics.title: Swapping, grouping and evaluating with terms
topics.ncert_sections: 2.2 (Swapping and Grouping, More Expressions and Their Terms)

concepts.learning_objective: Explain that adding terms in any order or grouping gives the same sum.
Evaluate an expression by first evaluating each term and then adding the terms.

topics.title: Removing brackets I and tinkering the terms
topics.ncert_sections: 2.2 (Removing Brackets I, Tinker the Terms I)

concepts.learning_objective: Remove brackets correctly, changing the signs of the terms when the bracket is preceded by a minus sign.
Predict how the value of an expression changes when one of its terms is increased or decreased.

topics.title: Removing brackets II: the distributive property
topics.ncert_sections: 2.2 (Removing Brackets II, Tinker the Terms II)

concepts.learning_objective: Use the fact that a multiple of a sum or difference equals the sum or difference of the multiples.
Use the distributive property to find products quickly by splitting a number.

topics.title: The Need for Smaller Units and A Tenth Part

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why a unit is split into smaller equal parts to measure lengths more exactly.
Express and read lengths as units and one-tenths, and convert between mixed and tenths forms.
Add and subtract lengths in units and tenths, regrouping 10 tenths as 1 unit.
Relate one-hundredths to one-tenths and units and write lengths using hundredths.
Compare lengths written with tenths and hundredths.
Add and subtract quantities in units, tenths and hundredths with regrouping.
Explain how the Indian place value system is extended to tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
Write quantities given in units, tenths and hundredths in decimal notation.
Read decimal numbers correctly, digit by digit after the decimal point.
Convert between millimetres, centimetres and metres using decimals.
Convert between grams and kilograms using decimals.
Convert between paise and rupees using decimals.
Locate decimal numbers on a number line divided into equal parts.
Recognise that zeros on the right of the last decimal digit do not change the value.
Compare decimals place by place and find the decimal closest to a given number.
Add decimal numbers by aligning place values and regrouping.
Subtract decimal numbers by aligning place values and regrouping.
Identify the rule of a decimal sequence and extend it.
Explain how misplacing a decimal point or mixing units changes a quantity.
Interpret notations such as hours and cricket overs that look decimal but are not based on ten.
Recall key steps in the history of decimal notation and the decimal separator.
Use letters to stand for numbers and recognise expressions containing them as algebraic expressions.
Write an algebraic expression or formula that describes a relationship given in words or in a situation.

topics.title: Revisiting Arithmetic Expressions and Omitting the Multiplication Symbol

concepts.learning_objective: Evaluate arithmetic expressions by writing them as sums of terms and handling brackets with a negative sign outside.
Find the value of an algebraic expression such as 5m + 3 by replacing the letter-numbers with numbers.
Identify like and unlike terms and add like terms into a single term.
Simplify expressions by removing brackets, using the distributive property and grouping like terms.
Decide whether two algebraic expressions are equal by comparing the values they take.
Find and apply the formula of a number machine from its inputs and outputs.
Describe the positions of items in a repeating pattern with expressions such as 3n - 1.
Use letter-numbers to prove that a calendar pattern always holds.
Find the general rule for the number of matchsticks at any step of a growing pattern.
Model real-life situations such as journeys and movement with algebraic expressions and interpret them.

topics.title: Intersecting lines: linear pairs and vertically opposite angles

concepts.learning_objective: Use the fact that a linear pair formed by two intersecting lines adds up to 180° to find unknown angles.
Identify vertically opposite angles and reason why they are always equal.
Explain why measured angles may differ slightly from values found by geometric reasoning.
Recognise perpendicular lines as intersecting lines that form four right angles.
Describe parallel lines as lines in the same plane that never meet however far they are extended.

topics.title: Parallel and perpendicular lines in paper folding; notation

concepts.learning_objective: Identify and count parallel and perpendicular creases formed by folding a square sheet.
Read and use arrow marks for parallel lines and the square mark for perpendicular lines.
Describe the eight angles formed when a transversal cuts two lines and the number of distinct measures possible.
Use equality of corresponding angles to find angles and to decide whether two lines are parallel.
Draw parallel lines with a ruler and set square and justify them using equal corresponding angles.
Make a line parallel to a given line through a point by folding two perpendiculars, and justify it.
Find alternate angles formed by a transversal on parallel lines and justify that they are equal.
Use the fact that interior angles on the same side of a transversal on parallel lines add up to 180°.
Find the number each person calls out when the rule is 'count the taller people in front of you'.
Judge whether statements about the called-out numbers are always, sometimes or never true.

topics.title: Picking Parity: Sums of Even and Odd Numbers

concepts.learning_objective: Explain parity using the idea of arranging a number in pairs.
Decide the parity of a sum from the parity and count of the numbers added.
Use the fact that two consecutive numbers have different parity.

topics.title: Parity in Grids and Expressions
topics.ncert_sections: 6.2 (Small Squares in Grids, Parity of Expressions)

concepts.learning_objective: Find the parity of the number of small squares in a grid without multiplying.
Identify expressions that are always even, always odd, or either.
Use 2n and 2n - 1 to find the nth even and nth odd number.

topics.title: Grid Sums and 3 x 3 Magic Squares

concepts.learning_objective: Use the smallest and largest possible sums and the total 45 to reason about grids filled with 1-9.
Explain why a 1-9 magic square has magic sum 15, centre 5, and 1 and 9 in middle positions.

topics.title: Generalising Magic Squares and Their History
topics.ncert_sections: 6.3 (Generalising a 3 x 3 Magic Square, Magic Squares in History and Culture)

concepts.learning_objective: Use the centre number m to describe a magic square and its magic sum 3m.
Predict the new magic sum when every number of a magic square is changed in the same way.
Recall the Chautisa Yantra and other magic squares in Indian history and culture.
Extend the Virahanka sequence by adding the two previous terms.
Count rhythms of short and long syllables, or 1-and-2 step paths, using the Virahanka numbers.
Recall who first described these numbers and the parity pattern of the sequence.
Solve simple cryptarithms by reasoning about place value and carries.
Apply parity to decide everyday puzzles such as switch toggling.

chapters.title: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines

topics.title: Equilateral triangles and constructing a triangle from its three sides

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the vertices, sides and angles of a triangle and name them correctly.
Construct a triangle from three given sides using intersecting compass arcs and explain why it works.

topics.title: Triangle inequality and existence of a triangle

concepts.learning_objective: Use the triangle inequality to decide whether three lengths can be the sides of a triangle.
Find possible lengths of the third side when two sides of a triangle are given.
Relate the sum of the two smaller lengths to whether the construction circles touch, miss or intersect.

topics.title: Constructing triangles when some sides and angles are given

concepts.learning_objective: Construct a triangle when two sides and the included angle are given.
Construct a triangle when two angles and the included side are given.
Decide whether two given angles on a base can form a triangle using their sum.

topics.title: Angle sum property and exterior angles

concepts.learning_objective: Use the angle sum property to find an unknown angle of a triangle.
Explain the proof of the angle sum property using a line parallel to the base.
Find an exterior angle of a triangle and relate it to the two opposite interior angles.
Define an altitude and locate it for acute, right and obtuse triangles.
Construct or fold an altitude and justify why it is perpendicular to the base.
Classify triangles as equilateral, isosceles or scalene from their sides.
Classify triangles as acute-angled, right-angled or obtuse-angled from their angles.

topics.title: Multiplying a fraction and a whole number

concepts.learning_objective: Multiply a fraction by a whole number by dividing the whole number by the denominator and multiplying by the numerator.
Find a whole number times a fraction as repeated addition and express the result as a mixed fraction.

topics.title: Multiplying two fractions using the unit square

concepts.learning_objective: Represent the product of two fractions as the area of a rectangle inside a unit square.
Use the rule 1/b x 1/d = 1/(b x d) for multiplying two unit fractions.

topics.title: Brahmagupta's formula, cancelling and order of multiplication

concepts.learning_objective: Apply the formula a/b x c/d = (a x c)/(b x d), including for mixed fractions and whole numbers.
Cancel common factors of numerators and denominators before multiplying to get the product in lowest form.
Recognise that the order of multiplying two fractions does not change the product.

topics.title: Is the product always greater than the numbers multiplied?

concepts.learning_objective: Predict that multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 gives a product less than the other number.
Predict that multiplying by a number greater than 1 gives a product greater than the other number.
Find the reciprocal of a fraction and use it to restate a division as a multiplication.
Divide fractions using a/b divided by c/d = (a x d)/(b x c).
Predict that dividing by a number between 0 and 1 gives a quotient greater than the dividend.
Predict that dividing by a number greater than 1 gives a quotient less than the dividend.
Choose and carry out the correct fraction operation in everyday and historical word problems.
Find what fraction of a whole figure a shaded region occupies by multiplying successive fractions.
Solve classical Indian fraction problems such as the dramma donation from the Lilavati.
